worst_places.before: `ExecutionContext` — абстракция над текущим входящим запросом, доступная в Guards, Interceptors и Exception Filters. Абстракция нужна потому что NestJS работает с несколькими транспортами: HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, Microservice RPC. Один и тот же Guard должен работать независимо от транспорта.
worst_places.after: `ExecutionContext` — обёртка над текущим входящим запросом. Её получают три вида перехватчиков Nest: Guard (решает, пускать запрос или нет), Interceptor (оборачивает вызов обработчика) и Exception Filter (превращает исключение в ответ клиенту). Обёртка нужна потому, что один и тот же Guard должен работать на любом транспорте — по транспортом здесь понимается канал, по которому пришёл запрос: HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC или RPC-сообщение микросервиса (RPC — remote procedure call, вызов метода на другом сервисе).

worst_places.quote: Setting it too high doesn't increase throughput past what the database itself can handle — Postgres has its own hard connection ceiling — and just moves the bottleneck from "waiting for a pool slot" to "the DB rejecting connections." A pool sized for peak concurrent queries per instance, multiplied by the number of horizontally-scaled instances, has to stay under the DB's `max_connections`; this is why high-replica-count deployments often need something like PgBouncer sitting between the app and Postgres rather than each instance holding its own large pool.
worst_places.problem: nestjs-q-38's connection-pooling paragraph: an 85-word sentence with an em-dash aside inside it, followed by a 55-word sentence built from a stacked noun phrase ("A pool sized for peak concurrent queries per instance, multiplied by the number of horizontally-scaled instances") plus a semicolon-joined second clause. 49.8% of all sentences in the en bank exceed 25 words (185 of 485 in ru), and the pitfall paragraphs are the worst offenders. Each of these sentences carries three separate facts that need three sentences.
worst_places.before: Setting it too high doesn't increase throughput past what the database itself can handle — Postgres has its own hard connection ceiling — and just moves the bottleneck from "waiting for a pool slot" to "the DB rejecting connections." A pool sized for peak concurrent queries per instance, multiplied by the number of horizontally-scaled instances, has to stay under the DB's `max_connections`; this is why high-replica-count deployments often need something like PgBouncer sitting between the app and Postgres rather than each instance holding its own large pool.
worst_places.after: Setting it too high does not buy you throughput. Postgres has its own hard connection ceiling, so a bigger pool only moves the bottleneck: instead of waiting for a pool slot, requests now get connections rejected by the database. Size the pool for one instance's peak concurrent queries, then multiply by how many instances you run. That total must stay under the database's `max_connections`. This is why deployments with many replicas usually put PgBouncer between the app and Postgres, instead of giving every instance its own large pool.

worst_places.quote: из-за чего Kubernetes помечает по-настоящему здоровый, но слегка медленно отвечающий под текущей нагрузкой под как not-ready
worst_places.problem: nestjs-q-45's pitfall paragraph, 66 words in one sentence. Inside it the word «под» appears twice in two different meanings back to back — first as the preposition in «под текущей нагрузкой», then as the noun "pod" — so «нагрузкой под как not-ready» reads as a typo and forces a re-read. worst_places.before: **Частая ловушка:** слишком агрессивно настроить `initialDelaySeconds`/`periodSeconds` readiness-пробы относительно того, сколько реально занимает проверка зависимости под нагрузкой, из-за чего Kubernetes помечает по-настоящему здоровый, но слегка медленно отвечающий под текущей нагрузкой под как not-ready и убирает его из ротации именно в момент, когда он под нагрузкой, которая и сделала его медленным — создавая петлю обратной связи, где оставшиеся поды поглощают больше трафика, замедляются и тоже помечаются как not-ready.
worst_places.after: **Частая ловушка:** выставить `initialDelaySeconds`/`periodSeconds` readiness-пробы агрессивнее, чем реально занимает проверка зависимости под нагрузкой. Тогда Kubernetes видит здоровый под, который просто отвечает чуть медленнее обычного, и помечает его как not-ready. Под выбывает из ротации ровно в тот момент, когда он под нагрузкой — той самой, которая его и замедлила. Дальше начинается петля: оставшиеся поды принимают больше трафика, тоже замедляются и тоже становятся not-ready.

worst_places.before: **Common pitfall:** Deploying a multi-instance NestJS service with the default in-memory `ThrottlerStorage` and believing the configured limit is actually enforced, because it works correctly in every local/single-instance test and staging environment with one replica — the bug only manifests in production, under real horizontal scaling, and shows up as "why is this client able to hammer us well past the configured limit" rather than as an obvious startup or test failure.
worst_places.after: **Common pitfall:** deploying a multi-instance NestJS service with the default in-memory `ThrottlerStorage` and assuming the configured limit is really enforced. It is not, but every local test and every single-replica staging environment passes, because with one instance the in-memory counter is correct. The bug appears only in production, once you scale horizontally. And it does not look like a failure: nothing crashes at startup and no test goes red. It looks like "why can this client send far more requests than the limit we set?"

worst_places.quote:
import { InjectionToken } from '@nestjs/common';

export const JWT_SECRET = new InjectionToken<string>('JWT_SECRET');
worst_places.problem: `InjectionToken` is not a constructible class in NestJS — that is Angular's API. `@nestjs/common` exports `InjectionToken` only as a type alias for what may be used as a token, so `new InjectionToken<string>(...)` does not compile. A reader who copies this whole section (it is presented as the recommended fix for string tokens, and the interview-mistakes bullet repeats "InjectionToken рекомендован для кастомных токенов") gets a compile error and no way to tell whether the article or their own setup is wrong. The same invented API reappears in ru/04 and ru/10 (`const DATABASE_URL = new InjectionToken<string>('DATABASE_URL')`) and in all three en counterparts.

worst_places.quote: Interceptor реализует интерфейс `NestInterceptor` с методом `intercept(context, next)`. `next.handle()` возвращает `Observable<any>` — поток ответа контроллера. RxJS операторы (`map`, `tap`, `catchError`, `switchMap`) позволяют трансформировать этот поток до, после или вместо выполнения контроллера.
worst_places.problem: The section is titled "Что такое Interceptor и почему он использует RxJS", and this is the entire prose of the article's only section that has any prose. Four unfamiliar concepts arrive in three sentences — Observable, stream, RxJS, and four operators — and none is explained or given an analogy before the next one lands. Everything after this point is code: the later sections add `of`, `from`, `timeout`, cold Observables and `subscribe` with no prose at all, and the "холодный" Observable idea (the key to why an interceptor can skip the controller) is stated only in a bullet at the very end of the file.
worst_places.before: Interceptor реализует интерфейс `NestInterceptor` с методом `intercept(context, next)`. `next.handle()` возвращает `Observable<any>` — поток ответа контроллера. RxJS операторы (`map`, `tap`, `catchError`, `switchMap`) позволяют трансформировать этот поток до, после или вместо выполнения контроллера.
worst_places.after:
Interceptor реализует интерфейс `NestInterceptor` с единственным методом `intercept(context, next)`.

Внутри него `next.handle()` — это ещё не вызов контроллера, а «обещание вызвать»: Observable, то есть поток значений из библиотеки RxJS. Поток «холодный» — контроллер запустится только когда на этот поток кто-то подпишется, и подписывается сам Nest. Отсюда три возможности: сделать что-то до `next.handle()`, навесить обработку на результат через `.pipe(...)`, или вообще не вызывать `next.handle()` и вернуть свой поток.

Обработку навешивают операторами RxJS: `map` меняет значение в потоке, `tap` смотрит на значение, ничего не меняя, `catchError` перехватывает ошибку, `switchMap` подменяет один поток другим. Ниже — по одному примеру на каждый.

worst_places.quote: onApplicationBootstrap is called after all modules are initialized and the HTTP server (or microservice) has started listening. So 'Module initialized' always prints before 'App bootstrapped'.
worst_places.problem: nestjs-quiz-5's explanation puts `onApplicationBootstrap` after the server starts listening. The question bank of the same topic says the opposite — nestjs-q-17: "**OnApplicationBootstrap** — fires after *every* module in the app has finished `OnModuleInit`" — and article 10 spells out the order explicitly: "(4) вызов `onModuleInit()` хуков, (5) запуск HTTP адаптера (Express/Fastify)", i.e. the hook fires before `listen()`. nestjs-quiz-8's explanation in the same bank hedges differently again ("the application is ready to accept connections"). Three different answers to the same factual question, and the sentence that carries the whole point of the item is the wrong one.
worst_places.before: onApplicationBootstrap is called after all modules are initialized and the HTTP server (or microservice) has started listening. So 'Module initialized' always prints before 'App bootstrapped'.
worst_places.after: onApplicationBootstrap is called after every module in the app has finished onModuleInit — but still before the server starts listening for requests. That makes it the safe place for work that needs the whole dependency graph up. So 'Module initialized' always prints before 'App bootstrapped'.

The question bank is the opposite shape: its leads are excellent (C 4, only nestjs-q-22 opens with a code block instead of a sentence) but the sentences are long. 238 of 478 en sentences and 185 of 485 ru sentences exceed the threshold, the pitfall paragraph at the end of nearly every one of the 50 entries is a single 55-100-word sentence carrying three or four facts, and the en version is systematically harder than the ru one in both length and register ("the odd one out", "hammer us", "bolted onto", "racy read-then-write", "tanking throughput").

The quiz has structural defects independent of language, in three layers: (a) the answer is option 0 in 26 of 28 items, so "always pick the first one" scores 93%; (b) the correct option is the longest in 19 of 28 en items and 17 of 28 ru — less extreme than quiz/postgresql's 26 of 29, but still roughly 2.5x chance, with the correct option averaging 1.3x the mean option length and reaching 1.9x in nestjs-quiz-24; (c) 28 items cover about six distinct facts — Guard vs Interceptor four times (1, 6, 16, 26), providers vs exports four times (4, 10, 25, 28), Pipes vs Filters three times (13, 20, 30), lifecycle hook order six times (5, 8, 15, 19, 23, 29) — and touch none of what the articles actually teach (ExecutionContext, Reflector, custom decorators, dynamic modules, CQRS, microservices, AsyncLocalStorage).
